title: RARE Scholars Charting New Paths in Medicine, Advocacy, Leadership and Business
summary: Learn how six students are using their experiences living with rare genetic conditions to bring fresh perspectives to their fields and advocate for others.
body_markdown:
When Amanda Beedle’s daughters were diagnosed with CLN2 disease, an ultra-rare neurodegenerative condition that belongs to a group of disorders called Batten disease, her life changed in an instant.


“The day we received the diagnosis was the last traditional shift I ever worked,” recalls Amanda, who had spent the past 10 years in healthcare as a registered nurse.


That day marked a turning point for Amanda, who initially stopped working to focus on supporting the needs of two children living with a rare genetic condition that historically has led to premature death by early adolescence. Connecting with others in the rare disease community eventually drew her into advocacy and, more recently, back to school. She is currently working on a Master of Science in nursing research through an online program offered by Cleveland State University.


Amanda is part of the 2026-27 cohort of BioMarin’s RARE Scholars program, which since 2018 has provided financial support to U.S. college students living with rare genetic conditions, including achondroplasia, Batten disease, mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) and phenylketonuria (PKU). In 2026, the program expanded to include caregivers, such as Amanda. Since its inception, RARE Scholars has awarded nearly $250,000 to more than 35 individuals who have demonstrated leadership in school and community activities.


Amanda has spent the past several years trying to balance medical appointments, school activities, family time and her work as a rare disease advocate. She says she never lost the connection to her work in healthcare and that influenced her decision to return to school.


“As I became immersed in the rare disease community, I realized there was an opportunity to use my clinical background and lived experience to help others,” she says. “Pursuing graduate school was a dream, but the realities of caring for a family affected by a rare disease made that dream uncertain. This scholarship helped provide an opportunity I might not otherwise have had.”
